books.section: Topic 1.3 European Exploration in the Americas
The Early Colonial Era: Spain Colonizes the New World

options.text: Portugal believed the earth was flat and the voyage would fall off the edge.
options.misconception: Scholars knew the earth was round; the dispute was over its size, and Portugal's experts did the math correctly.

options.text: Spain had more ships and more sailors than Portugal at the time.
options.misconception: Portugal was the leading seafaring power of the age; Spain was the newcomer to ocean voyages.

options.text: Columbus was Spanish, so the Spanish crown trusted him at once.
options.misconception: Columbus was Genoese, an Italian; Spain backed him after years of lobbying, not because of where he was born.

options.text: Portugal already had an African sea route to Asia; Spain had none.

rationales.A: The flat-earth story is a myth. Fifteenth-century scholars knew the earth was round; Portugal's experts rejected Columbus because his distance estimate was wrong.
rationales.B: The balance ran the other way. Portugal led Europe in seafaring; Spain's ocean fleet was small, and its kings were newcomers to the game.
rationales.C: Columbus was born in Genoa, in Italy. Spain backed him after years of lobbying, not because of where he was born.
rationales.D: Portugal's ships were already rounding Africa toward India, so a westward gamble looked pointless. Spain, newly unified after Granada, had no eastern route and everything to gain from a new one.
rationales.general:
1. Ask what Portugal already had. A working sea route to Asia, rounding Africa.
2. Ask what Spain had. No route east, a newly unified kingdom, and a king and queen willing to gamble.
3. Ask what Columbus offered. A shorter westward route, built on a wrong guess about the earth's size.
4. Rule out the rest. No one feared a flat earth, Portugal led at sea, and Columbus was Italian.
Remember: a gamble looks different to a country that already has a route.

stem: Why did Portugal turn Columbus down while Spain funded his voyage?

stimulus.source_note: Original secondary passage written for this question, from Barron's Premium 2027, Chapter 3, Topic 1.3, and 5 Steps to a 5 2024, Chapter 6, The Europeans Arrive.
stimulus.text: By the late 1400s, several forces pushed Europeans across the Atlantic. Asian spices and silk fetched high prices, and after the Ottoman Turks took Constantinople in 1453 the old land routes grew costlier and less certain. Spain had just finished the Reconquista with the fall of Granada in January 1492, and its crusading energy looked for new fields. Crowns raced each other for glory and territory. New ships and instruments, the caravel, the compass, and the astrolabe, made long ocean voyages possible for the first time.
